entry: Series of paintings, pastels and lithographs by Norwegian artist [[Edvard Munch]], first created in 1893 and later repeated in different versions. Its agonized central figure has become one of the most iconic images in art, seen as representing existential dread. Munch recalled a sunset walk above Oslo when the clouds turned "a blood red" and he sensed an "infinite scream passing through nature." Scholars dispute explanations for the orange sky, including the Krakatoa eruption, noting that Munch was not primarily interested in literal renderings. A Peruvian mummy that Munch could have seen at the 1889 Exposition Universelle has been suggested as an inspiration for the figure. Both painted versions were stolen from museums and later recovered. In 2012 a pastel version sold for the highest nominal price then paid for an artwork at public auction.

1957 Swedish historical film written and directed by [[Ingmar Bergman]]. Set in medieval Sweden during the [[Black Death]], it follows the knight Antonius Block, played by [[Max von Sydow]], who returns from the [[Crusades]] and challenges Death to a game of [[Chess|chess]] to delay his fate. The title refers to the seventh seal in the [[Book of Revelation]], and the silence that follows its opening reflects the film's theme of "the silence of God." Its final "Dance of Death" sequence became one of the most recognizable images in film history. The film won the Special Jury Prize at the 1957 Cannes Film Festival, establishing Bergman's international reputation. It has a 93% approval rating on [[Rotten Tomatoes]], and in 1958 [[The New York Times]] critics voted it one of the year's ten best foreign films.

1994 American prison drama film written and directed by Frank Darabont, based on a novella by [[Stephen King]]. [[Tim Robbins]] plays Andy Dufresne, a banker sentenced to [[Life imprisonment|life imprisonment]] for the murders of his wife and her lover, despite his claims of innocence. He befriends fellow inmate Ellis "Red" Redding, played by [[Morgan Freeman]]. Released by [[Columbia Pictures]] in 1994, the film was a box-office disappointment at first. It received seven nominations at the 67th [[Academy Awards]] and became the top video rental of 1995. It was selected for the National Film Registry in 2015.

1980 psychological horror film produced and directed by [[Stanley Kubrick]], co-written with Diane Johnson. Adapted from a 1977 novel by [[Stephen King]], it stars [[Jack Nicholson]] as a recovering alcoholic who becomes winter caretaker of a remote mountain hotel with his wife and clairvoyant son. Released in May 1980 by Warner Bros., it received mixed reviews, and about 27 minutes was cut across its theatrical versions. King criticized its departures from the novel and produced his own miniseries adaptation in 1997. It has since been reappraised as one of the greatest horror films.

1991 American psychological horror thriller directed by Jonathan Demme and adapted from Thomas Harris's 1988 novel. [[Jodie Foster]] plays FBI trainee Clarice Starling, who seeks the help of the imprisoned cannibal [[Hannibal Lecter]], played by [[Anthony Hopkins]], to track a [[Serial killer|serial killer]] known as "Buffalo Bill." It grossed $272.7 million worldwide on a $19 million budget. At the 64th [[Academy Awards]] it won the "Big Five" categories, and it remains the only horror film to win Best Picture. Some critics argue that its portrayal of Buffalo Bill perpetuates harmful stereotypes about gender identity;

American animated sitcom created by [[Matt Groening]] for the [[Fox Broadcasting Company]]. Set in the fictional town of Springfield, it satirizes American life through the Simpson family: Homer, Marge, Bart, Lisa and Maggie. The characters began as animated shorts on *The Tracey Ullman Show* in 1987, and the half-hour series premiered on December 17, 1989. It is the longest-running American animated series, sitcom and scripted primetime series, with 816 episodes broadcast. Its early 1990s seasons are generally considered its golden age, and [[Time (magazine)|Time]] named it the 20th century's best television series. Critics have described a decline in quality since then. The show has won 37 Primetime Emmy Awards. The Simpson family received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 2000, and Homer's catchphrase "D'oh!" has entered the [[English language]].

American [[Alternative rock|alternative rock]] band formed in [[Chicago]] in 1988 by Billy Corgan and bandmates. Its densely layered sound drew on heavy metal, grunge, [[Shoegaze|shoegaze]] and psychedelic rock. The albums *Siamese Dream* (1993) and *Mellon Collie and the Infinite Sadness* (1995), the latter a double album that debuted atop the Billboard 200, made the band one of the most commercially successful of the 1990s, with 30 million albums sold worldwide. The band disbanded amid internal conflicts, drug use and diminishing sales. It reunited in 2006 with Corgan as its only constant member. The band has won two Grammy Awards.

English rock band formed in [[Manchester]] in 1982, consisting of Morrissey, Johnny Marr, Andy Rourke and Mike Joyce. Morrissey and Marr formed the principal songwriting partnership. Signed to Rough Trade Records, the band released four studio albums between 1984 and 1987, including *The Queen Is Dead* (1986), which has appeared on several lists of the greatest albums of all time. Marr's bright guitar playing contrasted with Morrissey's baritone vocals and sardonic lyrics about social alienation and unrequited love. Internal tensions contributed to the band's breakup in 1987. The band is credited with influencing indie rock and Britpop.

1964 painting by Belgian surrealist [[René Magritte]], and perhaps his best-known work. Magritte painted it as a self-portrait: a man in an overcoat and bowler hat stands before a low wall overlooking the sea, his face hidden by a floating green apple, though his eyes remain visible. Magritte said the work reflects his interest in what the visible hides. [[Norman Rockwell]] created the homage *Mr. Apple* in 1970, replacing a man's head with a red apple. The painting also appears in the 1999 film *The Thomas Crown Affair*.

American crime drama television series created by David Chase for [[HBO]]. It follows Tony Soprano, played by [[James Gandolfini]], a [[New Jersey]] Mafia boss who begins [[Psychotherapy|psychotherapy]] for panic attacks while balancing his family life with his criminal activities. The series aired on HBO from January 10, 1999, to June 10, 2007, over six seasons and 86 episodes, and was primarily filmed at Silvercup Studios in New York City. Its portrayal of [[Organized crime|organized crime]] and Italian-American identity has drawn extensive critical analysis. Media commentators have credited it with ushering in a second golden age of television. It won 21 Primetime Emmy Awards and five Golden Globe Awards. Its abrupt final cut to black remains the subject of debate.

Novel by [[William Faulkner]], published in 1929. It is Faulkner's fourth novel, the second set in Yoknapatawpha County and the first to feature the Compson family. It centers on the siblings Quentin, Benjy, Jason and Caddy as their wealthy family in [[Mississippi]] descends into chaos. Each sibling's problems affect the others, from Benjy's mental disability to Caddy's promiscuity. Most of the action takes place over a single weekend in 1928, and the family's history emerges through sudden flashbacks. Its stream-of-consciousness narration and unreliable narrators are hallmarks of modernist literature. The novel sold poorly at first, but its reputation grew after Faulkner's novel *Sanctuary*, and it helped Faulkner win the 1949 Nobel Prize in Literature. Its title comes from a soliloquy in [[Macbeth]].

1965 American musical drama film produced and directed by Robert Wise, from a screenplay by Ernest Lehman. Starring [[Julie Andrews]] and [[Christopher Plummer]], it is a fictional retelling of Maria von Trapp's time as governess to seven children in [[Salzburg]], her marriage to Captain Georg von Trapp, and the family's escape during the [[Anschluss]] in 1938. It adapts the 1959 stage musical by Richard Rodgers and Oscar Hammerstein II. Released by 20th Century-Fox in March 1965, it became the highest-grossing film of 1965 and, by November 1966, the highest-grossing film in history, surpassing [[Gone with the Wind (film)|*Gone with the Wind*]]. It sold 283 million admissions worldwide and earned $286 million in total. The film won five Academy Awards, including Best Picture and Best Director.

Epic post-apocalyptic dark fantasy novel by [[Stephen King]], first published in 1978. Its plot centers on a deadly pandemic of weaponized [[Influenza|influenza]] and on survivors who gather into factions led by personifications of good and evil. King began it in 1975 in the spirit of *The Lord of the Rings*, and it introduced Randall Flagg, his recurring antagonist. The 1990 Complete & Uncut Edition restored over 300 pages. At 1,152 pages, it is King's longest stand-alone work. [[Time (magazine)|Time]], *Rolling Stone* and the BBC have included it among the best books of all time.

National anthem of the [[United States]], with lyrics by Francis Scott Key. Key wrote the poem "Defence of Fort M'Henry" on September 14, 1814, after watching the bombardment of [[Baltimore]]'s Fort McHenry by the British [[Royal Navy]] during the [[War of 1812]]. He set it to the tune of a popular British club song composed in [[London]] by John Stafford Smith. The song was first recognized for official use by the United States Navy in 1889. Congress made it the official national anthem by joint resolution, signed into law by President [[Herbert Hoover]] on March 3, 1931.

Oil-on-canvas painting by Dutch Post-Impressionist [[Vincent van Gogh]], painted in June 1889. It depicts the view from the east-facing window of his room at the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum near Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, just before sunrise, with an imaginary village added. Van Gogh had voluntarily admitted himself to the asylum in May 1889 and produced many paintings during his year-long stay. The celestial elements include [[Venus]], visible at the time, and a Moon whose depiction is not astronomically accurate. Scientific analysis has confirmed Van Gogh's use of [[Ultramarine|ultramarine]] and cobalt blue for the sky. The painting has been held by the [[Museum of Modern Art]] in New York City since 1941, acquired through the Lillie P. Bliss Bequest. It has been described as a "touchstone of modern art."

1942 French novella by [[Albert Camus]], also published in English as *The Outsider*. It follows Meursault, an indifferent man in French [[Algeria]] who kills an unnamed Arab man in [[Algiers]] weeks after his mother's funeral. The narrative is divided into two parts, presenting Meursault's first-person account before and after the killing. Published by Gallimard on May 19, 1942, during the Nazi occupation of France, the first edition was limited to 4,400 copies. [[Jean-Paul Sartre]]'s 1947 essay on the novel helped make it popular among anti-Nazi readers. Its philosophy of the [[Absurdism|absurd]] has been central to its reputation as a classic, although Camus rejected the [[Existentialism|existentialist]] label. [[Le Monde]] ranked it first on its list of the 100 Books of the 20th Century.

American rock band formed in [[New York City]] in 1998, led by vocalist Julian Casablancas, with guitarists Nick Valensi and Albert Hammond Jr., bassist Nikolai Fraiture and drummer Fabrizio Moretti. A leading group of the early-2000s garage rock revival, it released the debut album *Is This It* in 2001 to widespread critical acclaim. Its 2020 album *The New Abnormal*, produced by [[Rick Rubin]], won the Grammy Award for Best Rock Album. Its seventh album, *Reality Awaits*, was released on July 24, 2026.

1962 book by the philosopher Thomas S. Kuhn, published by the University of Chicago Press. Kuhn challenged the view that science progresses through the steady accumulation of accepted facts and theories. He argued instead that periods of "normal science" are interrupted by revolutions, in which accumulating anomalies lead to new [[Paradigm|paradigms]] that ask new questions and change the rules of research. He illustrated this with the Copernican revolution, which at first did not predict planetary positions more accurately than the Ptolemaic system. His claim that paradigm shifts are not logically determinate caused considerable controversy, and he addressed critics in a 1969 postscript. The book launched the word "paradigm" into widespread use, and it is a landmark in the history, philosophy and sociology of science.

American girl group formed in [[Detroit]] in 1959 as the Primettes. Signed to [[Motown]] in 1961 as the Supremes, they became the label's most commercially successful act, with twelve number-one singles on the Billboard Hot 100, more than any other American vocal group of the 1960s. Most of their hits were written and produced by Holland–Dozier–Holland. With [[Diana Ross]] as lead singer, the group later became Diana Ross & the Supremes under Motown president [[Berry Gordy]]. Ross left for a solo career in 1970, and the group, with changing members, disbanded in 1977. Its breakthrough is considered to have made mainstream success possible for later African-American R&B and soul musicians. Ross is the sole surviving original member.

Classic work of Japanese literature written by [[Murasaki Shikibu]], a noblewoman and lady-in-waiting, around the early 11th century. It is the first novel by a woman to win global recognition, and in Japan it has a stature similar to that of Shakespeare's works in English. The work depicts the lifestyles of high courtiers in the [[Heian period]]. It is written mostly in [[Hiragana|hiragana]] rather than the [[Kanji|kanji]] used for prestigious literature. Its hero, Hikaru Genji, is the emperor's son, but political considerations lead the emperor to demote him to commoner status. The original manuscript is lost, but more than 300 later copies survive. Arthur Waley's English translation, made between 1925 and 1933, omitted only one chapter. Complete translations have since been made by Edward Seidensticker, Royall Tyler and Dennis Washburn.

Play by [[William Shakespeare]], probably written in 1610–1611. Most of it is set on a remote island, where Prospero, a magician and the deposed Duke of [[Milan]], lives with his daughter Miranda, the spirit Ariel and the enslaved native Caliban. Prospero conjures a tempest that shipwrecks his enemies, including the King of [[Naples]]. The play explores magic, betrayal, revenge and forgiveness, and Prospero's renunciation of magic has been read as Shakespeare's farewell to the stage. It is listed in the First Folio as a comedy but has tragic elements, and criticism has classed it among his late romances. Its shipwreck draws on the 1609 grounding of the Sea Venture in [[Bermuda]].

1984 American science fiction action film directed by [[James Cameron]], who co-wrote it with producer Gale Anne Hurd. [[Arnold Schwarzenegger]] stars as a cyborg assassin sent from 2029 to 1984 [[Los Angeles]] to kill Sarah Connor, whose future son will lead humanity against the [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]] Skynet. Made for a $6.4 million budget, the film launched Cameron's career and established Schwarzenegger as a leading man. It spawned a franchise that includes [[Terminator 2: Judgment Day]] and a television series. It was selected for the National Film Registry in 2008.

1974 American [[Slasher film|slasher]] film directed by Tobe Hooper, who co-wrote it with Kim Henkel. Marketed as based on true events, it follows friends who encounter a cannibal family in rural Texas. Its killer, Leatherface, was inspired partly by the crimes of murderer [[Ed Gein]], but the plot is largely fictional. Made for under $140,000, it was a major commercial success. It was rated R, and it was banned in several countries. It grossed over $30 million domestically and is credited with originating the power tool as a murder weapon. It was selected for the National Film Registry in 2024.

1982 American science fiction horror film directed by [[John Carpenter]]. Based on John W. Campbell Jr.'s 1938 novella *Who Goes There?*, it follows researchers at an [[Antarctica|Antarctic]] station who face an alien life-form that imitates other organisms. Kurt Russell stars as a helicopter pilot. Released in June 1982 by [[Universal Pictures]] to negative reviews, it grossed $19.6 million, a weak result attributed partly to competition from [[E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial]]. Critics praised its creature effects, and the film later gained a cult following. It was selected for the National Film Registry in 2025.

Bronze sculpture by [[Auguste Rodin]] depicting a nude male figure of heroic size, seated on a rock and leaning forward with his chin resting on the back of his hand. Rodin conceived the figure for *The Gates of Hell*, a portal inspired by [[Dante Alighieri]]'s [[Divine Comedy]]. The first monumental bronze casting was made in 1904 and is exhibited at the Musée Rodin in [[Paris]]. Dozens of posthumous castings and several plaster versions exist, and casts are held in museums worldwide. The sculpture has become the iconic symbol of thinking, and its profile is often used to indicate [[Philosophy|philosophy]] and other practices of contemplation or introspection.
